Optimal number of clusters: Average silhouette method

Source: R/seg_prep.R
seg_nbclust_silhouette.Rd

Computes the average silhouette width for 2 to k_max clusters using factoextra::fviz_nbclust(). The silhouette width measures how well each respondent fits into its own cluster compared to the nearest other cluster. The optimal number of clusters maximizes the average silhouette width.

Usage

seg_nbclust_silhouette(
  x,
  cluster_method = c("kmeans", "hclust", "pam"),
  k_max = 10,
  nstart = 25,
  hc_method = "ward.D2",
  seed = 123
)

Arguments

x

The output of seg_prep_data() (recommended), or a data frame or numeric matrix with already prepared clustering variables (no missing values).

cluster_method

Clustering algorithm used to evaluate the solutions: "kmeans" (default, stats::kmeans()), "hclust" (hierarchical clustering via factoextra::hcut()) or "pam" (partitioning around medoids, cluster::pam()). k-means always uses Euclidean distances. NbClust does not support "pam" and is skipped in that case.

k_max

Maximum number of clusters to consider. Defaults to 10.

nstart

Number of random starts for k-means (WSS, silhouette). Defaults to 25.

hc_method

Agglomeration method for cluster_method = "hclust". Defaults to "ward.D2".

seed

Random seed. The global random seed is left untouched. Defaults to 123.

Value

A list with the elements method, optimal_k, criterion, values (tibble with the criterion per k) and plot (ggplot object).

Details

How it works

For each k, the respondents are clustered. For each respondent \(i\), \(a_i\) is the average distance to the other members of its own cluster (compactness) and \(b_i\) the average distance to the members of the nearest other cluster (separation). The silhouette width of the respondent is $$s_i = \frac{b_i - a_i}{\max(a_i, b_i)}$$ and the average silhouette width is the mean of \(s_i\) over all respondents. The silhouette is not defined for k = 1, so the method cannot indicate that there are no clusters. The distance matrix computed by seg_prep_data() is used if available.

Interpretation

Values of \(s_i\) close to 1 indicate respondents that are well clustered, values around 0 respondents between two clusters, and negative values respondents that are probably in the wrong cluster. For the average silhouette width, Kaufman and Rousseeuw (1990) suggest:

  • above 0.70: strong structure,

  • 0.51 to 0.70: reasonable structure,

  • 0.26 to 0.50: weak structure, could be artificial,

  • 0.25 or below: no substantial structure.

Attitudinal survey data mostly falls in the last category (values of 0.1 to 0.25 are common); segmentations can still be useful, but the segments then partition a continuum rather than separating natural groups. The silhouette method often favors k = 2; also look at the second-best k.

References

Kaufman, L. and Rousseeuw, P. J. (1990). Finding Groups in Data: An Introduction to Cluster Analysis. Wiley. doi:10.1002/9780470316801

See also

Other optimal number of clusters: seg_nbclust_gap(), seg_nbclust_indices(), seg_nbclust_wss()

Examples

# \donttest{
prep <- seg_prep_data(iris, vars = -Species, verbose = FALSE)
seg_nbclust_silhouette(prep)$plot

# }
